newsitem.title: USA: Once-dull real estate trusts attract Wall Street's eye.
newsitem.headline: Once-dull real estate trusts attract Wall Street's eye.

text.p: Real estate investment trusts (REITs), once seen as dull investments with sluggish growth prospects, have been showing new spark by raising heaps of cash in the risk-averse IPO market.
Smelling profits, real estate moguls Mort Zuckerman, Samuel Zell, and Australia's Frank Lowy are all planning IPOs to cash in on Wall Street's new-found admiration for the real estate trusts.
The trusts manage real estate portfolios such as shopping centres, office buildings, or hotels and pay high dividends, which can offer a cushion in a market downturn.

For the past year, real estate investment trusts returns including dividends beat the Standard & Poor's 500 Index with a 29.3 percent gain compared to the S&P's 25.13 percent, according to NAREIT, a Washington-based industry organisation.
"REIT IPOs have been doing a little better than expected. They are actually getting small pops, which is unusual," said John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket.

Two features boosting the star status of real estate investment trusts in today's market climate is their liquidity and high payout ratios. To keep their special federal tax status, they pay out 95 percent of their taxable income to shareholders.

Four of the real estate trusts have gone public in 1997, raising $674.7 million. Stock offerings of already-public real estate trusts are near chart-topping levels, raising $9.96 billion so far in 1997, well on their way to beating 1996's record $11.20 billion.

The four real estate investment trust stocks that went public this year gained on average 9.2 percent (excluding dividends) based on their Friday closing prices, better than their IPO counterparts. According to Fitzgibbon, 1997's IPOs have posted an average gain of 8 percent so far this year.

"The REITs have greatly improved their liquidity over the last three years," said Prudential senior real estate analyst Louis Taylor. "They still are not quite as liquid as utilities, but they have the highest absolute yield."

Taylor said with utilities providing relatively slim growth, many investors are using real estate investment trusts now for high income investments free from the queasiness inspired by Wall Street's daily rollercoaster rides.
With massive day-to-day fluctuations growing more common in the U.S. stock market, even brave investors are seeking safe havens to park pockets of their portfolio.

Zuckerman's Boston Properties Inc. has filed for a $737.5 million IPO, the biggest IPO yet this year and just shy of the top-grossing real estate investment trust IPO, the $750 million market debut of Rockefeller Centre Properties Inc. in September 1985.
Zell's Equity Office Properties Trust has filed for a $300 million IPO of 15 million shares to sell for $20 each.
Next week, a shopping mall real estate investment trust run by Lowy, the third richest man in Australia, plans a $300 million IPO of 18 million shares to sell for between $16 and $17.50 each.

The Lowy trust is called Westfield America and is based in Los Angeles. Analysts, who did not expect strong premiums on the Westfield trust in the first place, said its debut could be hurt by a critical Wall Street Journal report published Friday.
The report said many experts do not like Westfield's outside advisory structure. Under that arrangement, a separate outside adviser with different ownership will manage the company.
Analysts say, however, they do expect strong Wall Street interest in the Zuckerman and Zell offerings.
Real estate investment trusts and their IPOs have turned in mixed performances against the Standard & Poor's 500 over other time spans.

For 1997 through April 30, real estate trusts have lost 2 percent compared to the S&P's gain of 8.8 percent, according to NAREIT. They hold up better long term, with a gain of 15.8 percent compared to they S&P's 17 percent over five years.
The four real estate investment trusts IPOs that have gone public this year are Kilroy Realty Corp., Golf Trust of America, Cornerstone Realty Income Trust Inc. and Cornerstone Properties.
